text: Thanks for making time, Dana. Like I said at the counter, this is a free audit — I ask nosy questions for twenty minutes, then I put together a short report on what could be automated or taken off your plate. Sound fair?
Sounds fair. Fair warning though, it's a zoo in here today. We had a delivery mix-up this morning that ate half my day already.
That's actually a perfect place to start. What happened with the delivery?

So we run two trucks, Tuesdays and Fridays. The schedule lives on a paper calendar behind the register, and my delivery guy Marcus keeps his own version in his phone. This morning both trucks showed up at the same house for two different orders. The customer's standing in her driveway with two couches, and meanwhile the Hendersons across town got nothing and called me furious.
So a paper calendar and Marcus's phone. Who's supposed to be the source of truth?

The paper one, in theory. But if I'm with a customer and Marcus takes a delivery booking over the phone, he just types it in his notes app and tells me later. Sometimes later never comes. My daughter Ellie retypes it all into a spreadsheet on Sundays so we at least have a record.
How do customers find out when their delivery is coming? Do they get a reminder?

We call them the day before. Well — we're supposed to. Realistically it's me calling at eight at night when I remember, and if I don't reach them we just show up and hope. Probably one out of five deliveries, nobody's home and the truck goes back.
One in five bounced deliveries — okay, that's real money in truck time. I'm noting that one.
It drives me insane. Marcus bills me either way, obviously. He's a contractor.
Let's rewind to the front of the funnel for a second. When a new customer finds Hartwell, how does that usually happen?

Mostly word of mouth and drive-by, we've been on this corner thirty-one years. Facebook brings in more than I'd like to admit — people message the page asking if we have a sectional in stock, that kind of thing. And the phone still rings all day. Ellie set us up on Google somewhere along the way, so we get calls from that too.
The Facebook messages — who answers those, and how fast?

Whoever notices, honestly. Ellie checks it when she's in, which is three days a week. I've found messages from two weeks back asking about a dining set we had on the floor. By the time we answered, she'd bought one at Ashley. That one stung — that was a two-thousand-dollar table.
And phone calls when you're both tied up with customers — what happens to those?

It rings out to the machine. The machine's tape is usually full, I keep meaning to clear it. People don't leave messages anymore anyway — they just call the next store. I know we lose some that way, I just couldn't tell you how many.
That's one of the most fixable things you've said so far, for what it's worth. Okay — custom orders. You do special orders through the manufacturers, right? Walk me through one.

Sure. Customer picks a frame and a fabric on the floor, we write it up on a paper ticket, take a fifty percent deposit — usually on the Square — and I fax or email the order to the manufacturer depending on which one it is. Lead time's six to ten weeks. The ticket goes in the special orders binder, and when the truck shows up with the piece, we call the customer to schedule delivery and take the balance.
Between order and arrival, six to ten weeks — do customers hear anything from you in that window?

Only if they call us. And they do call — 'where's my order' is probably a third of the phone traffic some weeks. Ellie has to dig out the binder, find the ticket, sometimes call the manufacturer's rep, then call the customer back. Twenty minutes for a question that has a boring answer: it's coming in week seven.
A third of phone traffic is order-status calls. Beautiful. Not beautiful — but you know what I mean.
I'll take useful over beautiful at this point.
What about quotes that don't close on the spot? Say someone's deciding between you and Ashley on that dining set. Do you follow up?

We write the quote on a card and hand it to them. That's it. If they come back, they come back. My husband used to call people after a week, back when he ran the floor — he was shameless about it and honestly it worked. Nobody's done that since he passed. It feels pushy when I try.

I appreciate you sharing that. For the record, a friendly text two days later isn't pushy — and it doesn't have to be you sending it. Okay, let's talk money coming in. After a floor sale, that's Square at the register?

Floor sales, yes, Square handles it. Deliveries and custom balances are messier. Marcus can't take cards at the door, so it's checks or cash on delivery, or I call the customer and run their card over the phone into Square manually. Twice last month I forgot to run the balance until Ellie caught it doing the deposit.
So collecting final balances depends on you remembering to make a phone call.
Pretty much. There's probably a couple thousand floating out there right now that I just haven't gotten around to collecting. It's on a sticky note.
Do you invoice anyone — designers, landlords, commercial accounts — or is it all point of sale?

We've got maybe six decorators and a property management company that buy on account. I invoice them out of QuickBooks at the end of the month. Or the middle of the next month, depending on the chaos. The property company is slow to pay — sixty, ninety days sometimes — and chasing them is awkward because they're also my biggest account.
Who does the chasing when it happens at all?
Me. I write 'call Brightview about invoices' on the whiteboard, and it stares at me for three weeks. I hate that call more than anything else in this business.
You mentioned QuickBooks. Tell me about the books generally — who keeps them, how current are they?

My sister-in-law Pam does the bookkeeping. She's careful, but she's part time and she's in Arizona half the year. It's QuickBooks Desktop on the office computer — the 2019 version, before you ask, we never upgraded. Right now she's reconciled through... March, I think? So about three months behind.
And Square — do those sales flow into QuickBooks on their own, or does Pam key them in?

Pam keys them in from the Square reports. She prints them. There's a drawer of printed Square reports, I'm not proud of it. She says there's a way to connect them but she doesn't trust it, and honestly on Desktop 2019 I'm not sure it even works anymore.
When you want to know whether last month actually made money, what do you look at?

The checking account balance, honestly. Pam gives me a P&L when I ask but by the time I get it, it's telling me about a quarter that's already over. I run this place on vibes and the bank balance, which my accountant loves to remind me about every April.
You're in good company there. Does tax season hurt? Late nights, extensions, surprise bills?

We filed an extension the last two years. My accountant charges me extra to clean things up every spring — he calls it the 'shoebox surcharge'. I think it was eleven hundred dollars this year, just for the cleanup part.
Okay. Inventory — you mentioned a spreadsheet earlier for deliveries. What about stock? How do you know what's on the floor, what's in the warehouse, what to reorder?

There's a master spreadsheet Ellie built, and there's the truth, and they're related but not identical. We count the floor twice a year and it's a nightmare weekend both times. Reordering is me walking the floor going 'huh, we're low on recliners' and calling the rep. Last fall we sold out of the bestselling mattress for five weeks because nobody noticed we were down to one. Five weeks, our best mattress, at the start of holiday season.
Does the Square system know your inventory, or is it just a cash register to you?

It's a cash register. Ellie started loading items into it once, got about a third of the way through, then Christmas happened. So some things scan, most things get rung up as 'general merchandise' with a typed-in price.
Got it. Let's do the software inventory while we're at it. What do you pay for monthly — everything you can think of, even the embarrassing ones.

Square takes their cut per swipe. QuickBooks Desktop was a one-time thing forever ago. The website is on some builder — Ellie set it up — I think that's eighty-nine a month and it hasn't been touched since twenty twenty-three. There's also a marketing thing called Constant Contact we signed up for during COVID, that's like seventy-five a month, and I don't think we've sent an email in over a year. And I pay for a fax line. Don't laugh. Two of my manufacturers still want faxes.
No laughing. So roughly one sixty-five a month for a website and an email tool that aren't doing anything for you.
When you say it out loud like that it's worse. That's two grand a year for nothing.
The good news is that's budget we can point somewhere useful. Which tools do you actually like using?
Square, I like. It just works and I can see the day's take on my phone. Everything else I tolerate. QuickBooks I actively avoid — that's Pam's kingdom and I don't touch it.
Reviews. When someone loves their new sofa, do they ever end up saying so on Google? Do you ask?

We have... I want to say forty-some Google reviews? A couple of stinkers from delivery mix-ups sitting right at the top, which kills me because we've delivered to thousands of happy people. We don't ask. My husband thought asking was tacky and I guess I inherited that. Ashley HomeStore up the road has like nine hundred reviews.
Forty-something versus nine hundred, and you're competing for the same Google search. Do you ever reach back out to past customers? You've got thirty-one years of them.

There's a filing cabinet with every delivery ticket since the nineties, and whatever's in Square from the last few years. We've never emailed or mailed any of them. Every furniture person will tell you the cycle is seven to ten years — people who bought a bedroom set in twenty eighteen are due. I just have no way to reach them.
You do have a way, it's just trapped in a filing cabinet and a Square export. Okay, last stretch. Payroll — you, Ellie, anyone else? How does that get run?

Ellie and one floor salesman, Ray, plus Marcus who invoices me as a contractor. Payroll is me, a calculator, and the IRS withholding tables, every other Friday. Takes me about two hours and I redo the math twice because the one time I got it wrong, Ray reminded me for a month.
Two hours twice a month on manual payroll. And your own week overall — where do your hours actually go? Give me the honest version.

Honest version? I'm here six days, open to close, so sixty-five hours give or take. Maybe half of that is actually selling furniture, which is the part I love and the part that pays. The rest is phone tag, chasing deliveries, retyping things into spreadsheets, and Sunday nights I do the binder and the whiteboard and whatever paperwork piled up, usually two or three hours at the kitchen table. My kids call it 'mom's sad little office hour'.
If I could hand you back five hours a week, where would they go — business or kitchen table?

Kitchen table first. Then honestly, back on the floor. Every hour I'm on the floor we sell more, it's that simple. I'm the best closer here and I spend half my week being a very bad office administrator instead.
That's the whole case for this stuff, right there. Have you ever brought in help for any of this — an agency, a consultant, software someone sold you at a trade show?

Twice. A marketing agency out of Charlotte did our 'digital presence' a few years back — that was four hundred a month for stock photos on Facebook and a report I didn't understand. Cancelled after eight months. And a kid sold me a 'retail management system' at High Point market once. We paid the setup fee, forty-five hundred if I remember right, and it never got past the box of barcode labels. So I'm gun-shy, I'll tell you that upfront.

That's fair, and worth me knowing. My whole model is small pieces, one at a time, each one either pays for itself or we kill it. No forty-five-hundred-dollar boxes of labels. Last thing — is it just you making the call on something like this, or is Ellie part of it?

It's my name on the lease, so it's my call. But if Ellie hates a system it dies, because she's the one who'll actually run it. She's been begging me to modernize for two years, so you've got an ally there.
Good — I'd want her in the room when I show you the plan anyway. Anything I didn't ask about that eats your time or keeps you up?

The only other thing is the fabric protection plans. We sell them with most upholstery, there's a claims process when someone spills wine, and the binder for that is even worse than the special orders one. It's small money but it's the same disease — everything lives on paper and in my head, and I'm the bottleneck for all of it.

You said it better than my report will: everything lives on paper and in your head, and you're the bottleneck. Here's what happens next — give me a few minutes and I'll show you a one-page plan: what we heard, what I'd fix first, and what each piece roughly involves. Then you tell me what's interesting and what's not. No pressure either way.
Alright. Coffee's fresh if you want some while you do your magic. I'll go rescue Ray from the couple in the mattress section.
